title: In-Memory AM Demodulation Using an All-Silicon Independent-Dual-Gate Gain-Cell Memory with $<10^{-22}$ A Leakage Determined by Single-Electron Counting
authors: Katsuhiko Nishiguchi, Toshiaki Hayashi, Kensaku Chida, Takase Shimizu, Gento Yamahata, Seiya Kasai
abstract: Ultra-low-leakage memories are attracting increasing attention for in-memory sensing and computing. However, achieving sufficiently long retention in silicon memories for analog signal processing remains challenging because of leakage through the access transistor. In this work, we demonstrate an all-silicon independent-dual-gate memory whose leakage current, inferred from single-electron counting statistics, is below $10^{-22}$ A, giving a measured retention time exceeding 1000 s. Owing to the extremely low leakage, the subthreshold nonlinearity of the access transistor can be exploited without disturbing the stored charge, enabling in-memory amplitude-modulation (AM) demodulation. The proposed memory provides a CMOS-compatible platform for ultra-low-power signal processing and in-memory sensing.
summary: This paper presents an all-silicon, ultra-low-leakage memory device capable of in-memory signal processing. By achieving leakage currents below $10^{-22}$ A, the device enables the exploitation of transistor nonlinearity to perform Amplitude-Modulation (AM) demodulation directly within the memory array. This offers a highly energy-efficient, CMOS-compatible platform for advanced sensing and signal processing.
main_problem: The primary goal is to develop ultra-low-leakage memories suitable for performing in-memory Amplitude-Modulation (AM) demodulation, thereby reducing the need for external analog circuitry.
main_result: The proposed all-silicon independent-dual-gate memory achieved leakage currents below $10^{-22}$ A, enabling long retention and allowing the exploitation of subthreshold nonlinearity for successful AM envelope detection.
method: The authors measured leakage current using single-electron counting statistics and demonstrated AM demodulation by applying an AC signal and measuring the resulting time-averaged Signal-to-Noise (SN) voltage.
model_or_system: The system is an all-silicon independent-dual-gate memory (iDGCM) fabricated on SOI, which uses an intrinsic Si channel controlled by two gates to suppress leakage paths.
key_observables: Leakage current ($< 10^{-22}$ A), retention time ($> 1000$ s), Signal-to-Noise (SN) voltage dependence on input amplitude ($S_{amp}$), and the output envelope of the AM signal.
important_parameters: Leakage current ($< 10^{-22}$ A), retention time ($> 1000$ s), and the frequency relationship required for demodulation ($f_{mod} \ll f_{cutoff} \ll f_{carrier} - f_{mod}$).
main_assumptions: The leakage current measurement is an inference from single-electron counting statistics, and the analysis assumes the coupling between the Word Line and Upper Gate does not limit charge transfer in the relevant frequency range.
figures_summary: Figures illustrate the device structure, leakage characterization via single-electron counting, and the core demonstration: AC-to-DC conversion showing the frequency dependence of the SN voltage and the successful recovery of the AM signal envelope.
paper_structure: The paper first introduces the need for ultra-low-leakage memories. It then details the iDGCM structure and its superior leakage characteristics. The core of the work demonstrates the AM demodulation capability by exploiting the subthreshold nonlinearity, showing the frequency response and the final envelope detection.
why_interesting: While the physics is solid-state device physics, the concept of using fundamental electronic nonlinearities (subthreshold behavior) for signal processing in memory is relevant to energy-efficient quantum computing architectures that seek to integrate computation and storage.
